title: Saudi-Led Coalition Thwarts Two Missiles, Two Drones Over Riyadh, Al Jazeera Reports
body:
The Saudi‑led coalition announced on Tuesday that its air defenses successfully intercepted two missiles and five unmanned aerial vehicles that were launched toward Saudi territory, an attack it attributes to Yemen’s Iran‑backed Houthi rebels. The interceptions, which took place over several strategic sites across the kingdom, underscore a sharp escalation in the cross‑border hostilities that have intensified alongside fierce fighting in Yemen’s contested Marib and al‑Jawf provinces. The latest strike comes as the United Nations reports that more than 340,000 Yemenis have been forced to flee their homes since August, highlighting the growing humanitarian toll of the conflict.

The coalition’s statement said the missiles were detected by radar early in the morning and were neutralised by Patriot and Saudi “Patriot Advanced Capability” systems, while the drones were shot down by a combination of surface‑to‑air missiles and fighter aircraft. Officials did not disclose the exact locations of the interceptions, but they confirmed that no civilian casualties or damage to critical infrastructure were reported. The Houthi movement, which has been conducting a sustained missile and drone campaign against Saudi Arabia since late 2016, claimed responsibility for the launch, saying it was a retaliation for Saudi airstrikes in Yemen’s interior.

The incident marks the latest in a series of high‑profile attacks that have stretched the coalition’s defensive capabilities. In recent weeks, Houthi forces have intensified their operations in Marib, a key oil‑rich province that the Yemeni government has declared a “red line” for any further advances. Simultaneously, al‑Jawf, a northern governorate bordering Saudi Arabia, has seen heavy artillery exchanges and air raids that have displaced thousands of residents. Analysts note that the coalition’s ability to intercept the latest salvo demonstrates both the resilience of its air‑defence network and the growing sophistication of Houthi weaponry, which now includes longer‑range ballistic missiles and more autonomous drones.

Humanitarian agencies warn that the escalating violence is compounding an already dire crisis. The United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) estimates that the displacement surge since August has pushed the total number of internally displaced persons (IDPs) in Yemen to over four million, with many seeking shelter in already overcrowded camps in the north and west. Access to food, water, and medical services remains precarious, as ongoing clashes disrupt supply routes and impede aid deliveries. The coalition’s air strikes, while aimed at degrading Houthi command structures, have sometimes resulted in collateral damage, further complicating relief efforts.

Regional observers see the latest exchange as part of a broader proxy contest between Saudi Arabia and Iran, each backing opposing sides in Yemen’s protracted war. Tehran’s support for the Houthis—through arms transfers, training, and logistical assistance—has enabled the rebel group to acquire precision‑guided munitions and drone technology previously unavailable in the theater. Conversely, Riyadh’s coalition, bolstered by United Arab Emirates forces and Western intelligence, has sought to contain the rebel advance while maintaining the fragile legitimacy of Yemen’s internationally recognized government. The back‑and‑forth of missile and drone attacks risks drawing neighboring states deeper into the conflict, especially if the Houthis expand their targeting to critical energy infrastructure in the Persian Gulf.

Looking ahead, the coalition has pledged to strengthen its defensive posture and to continue air operations aimed at neutralising Houthi launch sites. Diplomatic channels, however, remain stalled; recent United Nations‑mediated talks in Kuwait have failed to produce a ceasefire agreement, and both sides have accused each other of violating existing de‑escalation accords. The next few weeks will be crucial in determining whether the conflict spirals into a broader regional confrontation or whether a renewed push for negotiations can curb the cycle of retaliation that has already displaced hundreds of thousands and left Yemen’s humanitarian situation at a breaking point.
